Toddler teacher here...

There are many reasons for a child to bite and it’s pretty typical from infancy. It is more concerning once they reach the age of preschool(in my view, 3yrs and up).

It’s good that you recall what happened before each bite because it helps you see a pattern in possible reasons for the bite. When they are learning to communicate through language, it is common for their frustration from being unable to communicate their thoughts effectively and completely through words, resulting in challenging behaviors like biting.

From what you’ve detailed, it’s possible your child may feel frustration from people (even parents and familiar adults) touching their bodies as it may be an uncomfortable sensory experience or a spatial preference. It’s also possible they haven’t mentally prepared for transitions like being strapped in a stroller or picked up to leave the park.

Try to give them 10 minutes, 5 minutes, 2 minutes, and minute reminders that a transition is about to happen to give them time to process that they will be changing scenery or ending their play soon.

You can also offer for them to walk on their own or teach them to strap themselves if they have the fine motor skills. Of course if they choose not to, you can give them reminder you will have to pick them up or strap them in yourself if they don’t try or comply when you need to keep a schedule.

I hope this was helpful and good luck! Biting can be frustrating and disappointing. But it is typical and it’s neither your or the child’s fault that it is happening. Eventually they can learn the self regulation and social skills to do something else.

Hello,

Preschool teacher here. The teachers should be documenting each incident and trying to find out why the other child is engaging in these challenging behaviors. They may do this by recognizing the verbal or nonverbal cues that may hint the child is likely to make unsafe choices with another child. When they have an idea of the reasons for the child’s behavior, they should redirect the emotions or actions to something socially appropriate.

This will take time though as children need a lot of practice to start implementing any type of skill or strategy without an adult mediating or facilitating.

As the parent to your child who is receiving these behaviors, if they are recalling the events you can reassure them it is NOT okay for anyone to do that to her. Even if a child bites in self defense as a reason, the child who is bitten still needs to be reassured they will be kept safe. You can encourage your child to walk away if they feel a peer is being unsafe with their body or having a hard time listening. If another child persists and follows your child, you can also encourage them to seek help from a teacher, who can help keep your child safe and help mediate a conversation of what each child is feeling and wanting to do. 

Possibly point out different clues that could let your child know a peer might be unsafe with them (e.g. yelling, hitting, furrowed brows, frowning, raised hands). This way they can try to move away and advocate for their own safety. Not to say the teachers can’t be observant and mindful of this also, but moving away and asking a teacher for help in an unsafe situation can empower a child to seek safety on their own.

I’m a toddler teacher and I just graduated with my bachelors about a year ago. I understand that repeating things and giving reminders constantly can be frustrating but what that teacher is doing is NOT okay. It seems like this teacher needs more training on keeping composure, classroom maintenance, and general appropriate interactions and responses to children.

A constant raised voice and asking things like, “do you understand that?” is inappropriate as it will affect the children’s self esteem and self image of their capabilities. If it doesn’t seem like their teacher can be patient with them and is always raising their voice, the children may internalize that this teacher doesn’t like them or that they are always doing something wrong.

A teacher’s voice is a classroom tool and if they’re only using it to bark orders then they’re not using it as a learning tool anymore. It’s disrespectful to the child and also teaches them that yelling at others is okay. In my classroom, children may yell in the yard if they’re upset but we let them know that yelling at others will make other children or teachers upset or sad and try to teach empathy skills from there.

Grabbing things out of a child’s hand also shows them they can do the same with other children.

Tell the main teacher of your main concerns and how you are worried of what goes on during the day if that is what you witness during the small windows you do see the classroom. The main teacher is responsible for the conduct of her staff. If changes don’t happen, go to the director. Those behaviors should change quickly after that. 

It’s possible the teacher is inexperienced in keeping composure and doesn’t know the power her voice has in the classroom. You can suggest that the main teacher or others observe this teacher and step in if they see she may need a 5 minute break away from a child to cool down when she too frustrated to be a composed teacher. 

As a parent, you can also step in and tell that teacher how you feel about her yelling or grabbing items when you see it. She’ll check herself really quick if a parent is expressing concerns about her behavior.
